title: What a Cooking Pot Can Tell Us
section: 讲话 / 报道 / 讲座
transcript:
Archaeologists sometimes learn more from the inside of a broken pot than from its decoration. Traces of fats and other substances can remain in the clay long after visible food has disappeared. These traces offer evidence about past cooking practices, but interpreting them requires care. A vessel may have been used for different foods at different points in its life.

In a university workshop, students examined fragments from an ancient settlement beside a river. Some fragments contained compounds associated with aquatic foods. It would have been tempting to conclude that fish dominated the inhabitants' diet. The instructor asked the class to consider what the collection actually represented. The pots came from one building, and the building may have served a specialised purpose.

The students compared the chemical findings with other evidence. Fish bones were present, but grinding stones and charred cereal grains were also common. Moreover, the largest pots showed signs of repeated heating, whereas smaller vessels contained a different mixture of residues. Together, these observations suggested varied activities rather than a single food source.

The instructor also explained a preservation problem. Some substances survive in clay more readily than others. The strongest chemical signal therefore need not represent the food consumed in the greatest quantity. Modern experiments, in which known ingredients are cooked in replica pots, can help researchers understand such differences, although they cannot reproduce every condition of burial.

The broader lesson is about the relationship between an object and a population. A residue provides direct evidence that a substance entered a particular vessel. Moving from that observation to a claim about an entire community requires additional steps. Archaeological explanations become stronger when independent forms of evidence support the same account.

questions.prompt: What difficulty does the speaker mention when interpreting food residues?
options: Pot decoration always identifies the exact recipe.
A pot may have held different foods over its lifetime.
Only complete pots retain any chemical traces.
All substances survive equally well in clay.
questions.answer: A pot may have held different foods over its lifetime.
questions.explanation: 同一容器在不同时期可能用于不同食物，因此残留物并非单次烹饪的简单记录。

questions.prompt: Why was it premature to claim that fish dominated the community’s diet?
options: The fragments came from one building that might have had a special function.
The settlement was located too far from water.
The researchers had found no traces of aquatic foods.
The pots were all modern replicas.
questions.answer: The fragments came from one building that might have had a special function.
questions.explanation: 陶片仅来自一栋可能有专门用途的建筑，不能直接代表整个群体的饮食。

questions.prompt: What additional evidence indicated a varied diet?
options: Paint used to decorate the largest pots.
The number of people attending the workshop.
Grinding stones and charred cereal grains.
The modern price of fish in nearby markets.
questions.answer: Grinding stones and charred cereal grains.
questions.explanation: 磨石和炭化谷物与鱼骨共同出现，说明食物来源不止鱼类。

questions.prompt: Why may the strongest chemical signal be misleading?
options: It always comes from an ingredient added after excavation.
It proves that a pot was never heated.
It identifies the most valuable food rather than the most common one.
Some substances survive better in clay than others.
questions.answer: Some substances survive better in clay than others.
questions.explanation: 不同物质保存能力不同，信号最强不等于当时食用量最大。
